#10595. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#10591. Find Orphan Pages and Buried Content: Build an Internal Link Graph for Your Site

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an important page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:

Wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:

We have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

#10590. Could Meta fix its glasses privacy issues with an LED redesign?

Meta launched its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

Meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the company’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

So this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

Does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

#10589. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

Nvidia is stuck between a rock and a hard place, as "irreplaceable talent" wants to leave if Jensen Huang isn't reinstated as CEO amidst the spy affair controversy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, there are warnings that important Nvidia employees are planning to leave if the company doesn’t reinstate him. According to the Wall Street Journal, an employee sent an internal letter to the top executives and board of directors stating that “failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’” Huang resigned last week amidst a firestorm of reports about an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a further affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell, and allegations the former relationship may have facilitated chip smuggling into China.

According to WSJ’s sources, director of developer technology Nader Khalil wrote the letter, urging that Huang be reinstated as CEO, lest the company lose loyal and important employees. The letter’s recipients, according to WSJ, comprised roughly 60 direct reports and the 10 members of the board, and Khalil warned that “Irreplaceable talent at Nvidia is now contemplating departing.”

The internal letter, along with the standwithjensen.com open letter to reinstate him, shows how important Huang is to the employees of Nvidia. Without the key long-term employees, which the company heavily depends on, progress could halt, or possibly regress, as Nvidia would lose the employees who have worked on and built the architectures and systems that make Nvidia what it is, along with their leader, Huang — who has recently stated that he would be honored to come back as CEO.

The open letter, signed by multiple Nvidia current and former employees, and tech CEOs and investors, states that employees are concerned that Huang was ousted unfairly and without due process, expressing that the employees do not have “access to the board’s private deliberations,” and that they have not been shown evidence that Alice Huang was indeed a spy, which even US intelligence doesn’t have solid evidence of. The open letter demands that Huang be reinstated as CEO while ensuring an independent investigation and a fair hearing, including providing a “specific, evidence-based explanation” of why Nvidia shouldn’t keep Huang as CEO — with Huang scheduled to appear before a House of Foreign Affairs panel concerning his affairs with the alleged spy.

Despite the letter, the support of other Silicon Valley CEOs, and even President Trump, Nvidia is still not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Nvidia is the hottest AI hardware company at the moment, and its employees are highly desirable not only within the US, but possibly China as well. China surely wouldn’t mind getting its hands on a few key employees, who, if they choose to leave, are likely not going to have a hard time finding another job.

#10579. Running an AI Agent on a Local LLM: What I Measured on One GPU

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

The agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you plan to run an agent on local hardware.

OpenClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

The Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

The extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:

On the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

OpenClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel showed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

The first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:

Reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

The speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the new tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

Ollama's documentation says models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

An embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

What this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

In this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

It handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly said its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

#10576. Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

Tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

When the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

Swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That said, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”

With audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

This had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an update, so here’s hoping.

I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

The experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

There is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

The best budget-friendly gifts for gamers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gamers in your life might be hoping for a $7,000 graphics card (I know I am), but that doesn't mean they won't still appreciate some solid, significantly cheaper gaming peripherals. While $80 doesn't go quite as far as it used to, there are still plenty of awesome accessories that any gamer would be thrilled to receive — including headsets, mice, keyboards, microphones, mouse pads, and even an Elgato Stream Deck.

Budget-friendly doesn't mean compromising on quality or convenience, either. While you won't be able to find all the bells and whistles at the sub-$80 level, there are both wired and wireless headsets, mice, and keyboards at this price point, including some last-generation flagship products. Razer's DeathAdder V3 Pro is currently on sale for $64.99, and remains one of the best-feeling mice we've ever tested — and its shape was so good that Razer kept it, exactly, in the newer DeathAdder V4 Pro. HyperX's Cloud III gaming headset is basically identical to our favorite Cloud III S headset — the only real difference is that the Cloud III is wired, while the Cloud III S is wireless.

The HyperX Cloud III is a wired gaming headset with a detachable microphone. It features 53mm drivers and virtual surround sound support.

This wireless lightweight over-ear headset weighs just 212g and is very comfortable. It features very good embedded beamforming mics and gets up to 24 hours of battery life on a single charge.

The G203 is now on sale for under $19 and is a great option for a budget mouse. It has six programmable buttons, and an 8K DPI optical sensor. There's also a RGB strip that wraps around the backside and shows off the Logitech "G" for a bit of bling.

Sporting a 12K sensor, a 99g weight, and a 250-hour battery rating on a single AA battery, Logitech's G503 wireless isn't an ultra-light 8K polling elite gaming mouse. But it solid experience while gaming and working. Unless you're playing competitive titles on an elite level, it just might be all the gaming mouse you really need.

Save an incredible 47% and get the Logitech G309 Lightspeed on sale for only $42.50. The G309 connects via Bluetooth or Wireless, uses a Hero 25K DPI sensor, six programmable buttons, and Lightforce mechanical switches.

The DeathAdder V3 Pro is a lightweight wireless gaming mouse with a fantastic shape, Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, and up to 90 hours of battery life. It weighs just 63g and is perfect for a range of gamers.

This Razer wireless gaming mouse features the company's Focus Pro 30K DPI optical sensor. It has a battery life of 280 hours using a single AA battery.

A wired membrane keyboard that punches above its weight: features SteelSeries' Whisper-Quiet membrane switches, 8 zones of RGB lighting, and a compact TKL form factor. It's also water- and dust-resistant.

Hexgears Immersion A3 combines the small footprint of a TKL keyboard with low-profile keycaps and switches, and multi-connectivity with 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth, plus a wired connection. There's even a small TFT screen to monitor battery life or host a personalized GIF.

The Logitech G413 TKL SE Mechanical Gaming Keyboard is a wired device with backlit keys. As the name suggests, it has a tenkeyless form factor so there is no numeric pad. The keys are mechanical with tactile switches.

This budget-friendly gaming mic features a unique ball shape and sounds fantastic out of the box. It comes with a sturdy desktop stand and features two mounting points so you can mount it at an angle, as well as a cardioid polar pattern and fun RGB lighting.

A USB condenser mic with a cardioid polar pattern, excellent sound out of the box, and a built-in desktop stand with a mounting point on the bottom. It also has a large tap-to-mute button on the top, and a red indicator light so you know when the mic is recording.

These 2.0 desktop speakers have a unique, round pebble shape with angled drivers so the sound hits your ears just right. They feature both wired and Bluetooth connections, have impressive bass for their size, and they've even got customizable RGB lighting around the base.

The Stream Deck Mini features six buttons but is otherwise compatible with the full suite of Stream Deck tools from Elgato.

SteelSeries' classic QcK gaming mouse pad is fairly basic — featuring a micro-woven cloth surface and a nonslip rubber backing, and measuring 12.6 x 10.8 inches (320 x 270mm) and just 2mm thick — but it's a solid option if you're looking for a no-frills mouse pad to up your mouse accuracy.

This XL extended mouse pad has a cloth surface that feels great — almost like a cooling pad. It features a non-slip rubber backing and a gunmetal gray pattern that may not be for everyone.

SteelSeries' performance-specific mouse pads are designed for specific scenarios — the balance mouse pad has a soft cloth surface designed to give you a mix of speed and precision.

The city is making its first major investment through the Community Benefit Ordinance, using a portion of the tax generated by SpaceX AI's Colossus 1 facility for the benefit of residents.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The City of Memphis has announced that it will make its first major investment as part of its new Community Benefits Ordinance. The fund will use revenue generated by taxing SpaceX AI's Colossus 1 facility to fund various initiatives within the South Memphis neighborhoods around that data center. The fund will help with the costs associated with housing, neighborhood improvements, and services, with the first $2 million allocated for the Memphis HOPE Initiative — a new home repair assistance program that helps residents make vital repairs as well as improvements that will make their homes more accessible.

The HOPE Initiative will provide low- and moderate-income homeowners and even renters with up to $25,000 for qualifying repairs and improvements. Eligible improvements include structural repairs as well as plumbing, heating, and air conditioning repairs. Roof repairs and replacement, accessibility improvements, and some exterior improvements like painting, fencing, and landscaping are also eligible. Funds will be provided as a deferred, interest-free, forgivable loan with zero monthly payments. Any required lien will be recorded after repairs are completed and forgiven after three years.

SpaceX AI's Colossus 1 data center became fully operational in May 2025, packing 220,000 GPUs and 300 megawatts of compute capacity. A year later, in May 2026, it was announced that Anthropic had signed a lease that would see it take over the entire facility in an effort to ease usage bottlenecks across Claude's paid-for ecosystem. The company said that the additional compute afforded by Colossus 1 would enable higher Claude Code limits, the removal of throttling for Pro and Max customers, and increased API request limits for Claude Opus models. But none of that will matter to those benefiting from the Community Benefits Ordinance, of course.

Today's news comes hot on the heels of SpaceX AI CEO Elon Musk telling employees that the company will increase the power capacity of its data centers by 7x to 10 gigawatts by late 2027. The move would see those data centers rake in between $300 billion and $500 billion per year, according to Musk. Perhaps notably, the claim also comes as SpaceX's market capitalization dropped by nearly $570 billion in less than two months.

#10571. Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

Over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

The answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild new AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

Perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

Ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

The main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

The same issue cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

Portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens issue or some weird setting.

Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

#10570. Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves You

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

Yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."

The bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is currently visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.

A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.

Nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.

China's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.

The truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.

Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.
